SQLAlchemy boolean comparisons should use `.is_(True)`/`.is_(False)` rather than `== True` (and avoid `# noqa: E712`). This produces clearer SQL and avoids lint suppression.

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body:
`push_environment` is nullable (and will be NULL for existing users after migration). Comparing with `!= settings.APNS_ENVIRONMENT` will skip those users entirely, so escalation pushes may silently never send until every client re-registers. Consider treating NULL as a default (e.g., assume current `APNS_ENVIRONMENT`) or backfilling existing rows in the migration.
```suggestion
            # Skip tokens registered for a different APNs environment.
            # Treat NULL as the current environment so legacy rows created
            # before push_environment existed still receive escalation pushes.
            if (
                helper.push_environment is not None
                and helper.push_environment != settings.APNS_ENVIRONMENT
            ):
```

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: The comment calls this a “Critical Alert”, but the payload isn't a critical alert per Apple spec (critical alerts require a special entitlement and `aps.sound` as a critical-sound dictionary). Either adjust the payload to a real critical alert or update the comment to avoid misleading future changes.

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body:
`push_environment` can be NULL for existing users; this strict equality check will prevent sending any push to those tokens. Consider treating NULL as the default environment (or migrate/backfill) so existing registered tokens still receive pushes.
```suggestion
        target_push_environment = (
            target.push_environment
            if target.push_environment is not None
            else settings.APNS_ENVIRONMENT
        )
        if target_push_environment == settings.APNS_ENVIRONMENT:
```

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body:
`aps.sound` is being set to `audio_url`, but APNs/iOS interpret `aps.sound` as a bundled sound name (or critical-sound dict), not a remote URL. Since `audio_url` is already included as a custom field, keep `aps.sound` as a valid value (e.g., "default") and let the iOS Notification Service Extension read `audio_url` from the custom field. Also, NSE execution requires `aps["mutable-content"] = 1`; without it, the extension won’t run to download/attach audio.
```suggestion
                    "sound": "default",
                    "content-available": 1,
                    "mutable-content": 1,
```

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body:
Defaulting `environment` to "sandbox" means older clients (or any client that omits the field) will register as sandbox even in production, and then will be skipped by the server-side `push_environment` checks. Consider making this field required, or default it based on server config, to avoid silently disabling pushes in production.
```suggestion
    environment: Literal["sandbox", "production"]
```

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: `APNS_ENVIRONMENT` is a free-form string; any typo will silently select the sandbox host. Consider constraining it (e.g., `Literal["sandbox","production"]` in Settings or a validator) and failing fast on invalid values so production doesn’t accidentally send to the wrong APNs endpoint.

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: The APNs clients are created without explicit timeouts. APNs calls in Celery tasks can then block longer than desired under network issues. Consider configuring a reasonable `httpx.Timeout` (and optionally limits/retries) when constructing the clients.

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: `apns.send_sync()` does network I/O while the async DB session is still open, which can unnecessarily hold a DB connection for the duration of APNs sends. Consider fetching the helper tokens first, closing the session, then sending pushes, and finally opening a new session only for stale-token cleanup (or otherwise ensure DB resources aren’t held during external calls).

title: feat: replace current_streak with solo_streak and inclusive_streak
author: GinoLin980

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body:
In `upgrade()`, the columns are added as nullable and only later backfilled + altered to NOT NULL. If the app (or any background job) writes to `users` while this migration is running, a row inserted between `add_column` and the `UPDATE` could keep NULLs and cause the `alter_column(..., nullable=False)` step to fail. Consider adding the columns with a temporary `server_default=0` (and optionally `nullable=False` immediately), then backfill `inclusive_streak` from `current_streak`, and finally drop the server default if you don't want it long-term.
```suggestion
    # 1. Add new columns with temporary defaults so concurrent inserts cannot create NULLs
    op.add_column(
        "users",
        sa.Column(
            "solo_streak",
            sa.Integer(),
            nullable=False,
            server_default=sa.text("0"),
        ),
    )
    op.add_column(
        "users",
        sa.Column(
            "inclusive_streak",
            sa.Integer(),
            nullable=False,
            server_default=sa.text("0"),
        ),
    )

    # 2. Preserve existing streak data from current_streak
    op.execute("UPDATE users SET inclusive_streak = current_streak")

    # 3. Drop temporary defaults now that data has been backfilled
    op.alter_column("users", "solo_streak", server_default=None)
    op.alter_column("users", "inclusive_streak", server_default=None)
```

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body:
The same nullable→backfill→NOT NULL pattern in `downgrade()` has the same risk if writes happen during the downgrade (rows could be inserted with NULL `current_streak` before it’s altered to NOT NULL). Consider using a temporary `server_default` during the downgrade as well, so concurrent inserts can’t violate the new constraint.
```suggestion
    op.add_column(
        "users",
        sa.Column(
            "current_streak",
            sa.Integer(),
            nullable=True,
            server_default=sa.text("0"),
        ),
    )
    op.execute("UPDATE users SET current_streak = inclusive_streak")
    op.alter_column("users", "current_streak", existing_type=sa.Integer(), nullable=False)
    op.alter_column("users", "current_streak", existing_type=sa.Integer(), server_default=None)
```

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: PR description says wrong-owner access to /verify should return 404 (to avoid leaking resource existence), but this test now asserts 403. Either update the implementation to return 404 for non-owners and keep tests aligned, or update the PR description if 403 is the intended contract.

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: Test DB setup uses `Base.metadata.create_all`, but the date-level uniqueness guard is implemented only as a raw SQL expression index in this Alembic migration. That means the Layer-2 idempotency behavior (same alarm + same day, different timestamps) won’t exist in tests unless migrations are applied or the index is also represented in SQLAlchemy metadata. Consider running Alembic migrations in tests or adding an equivalent SQLAlchemy `Index(..., unique=True, ...)` so test schema matches production.

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: create_wake_event() claims idempotency for “same alarm on the same calendar day”, but the tests currently only cover exact timestamp duplicates. Add a test that posts two different `scheduled_time` values on the same UTC date and asserts the second call returns 200 with the original event id (exercising the functional unique index + IntegrityError path).

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body:
In verify_wake_event(), the row is selected with `FOR UPDATE` even when `passed=False`, and then the function returns without committing/rolling back. This holds the row lock until the request/session ends and can block the timeout jobs (or other clients) from progressing the state machine. Consider avoiding `FOR UPDATE` for the no-op path (or explicitly `await db.rollback()` before returning) so locks are released immediately.
```suggestion
    if not passed:
        # We selected the row WITH FOR UPDATE; rollback so the lock is released immediately.
        await db.rollback()
```

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: In create_wake_event(), Job A is scheduled using wake_event.id before any flush. With `mapped_column(..., default=gen_uuid)`, the UUID is typically assigned during flush/INSERT, so `wake_event.id` may still be None here, causing Celery to receive args=[None] and Redis keys like `job:respond:None`. Generate the id explicitly (e.g., set wake_event.id before add) or `await db.flush()` before scheduling so a real id is available.

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: _fetch_existing_for_date() uses `func.date(timestamptz)` which depends on the DB session timezone, but the unique index added in the migration uses `(scheduled_time AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date`. After an IntegrityError from that index, this query may fail to find the existing row and re-raise unexpectedly. Align the query expression with the index (use the same UTC cast) so duplicates are reliably fetched.

title: feat: Wake Event API — State Machine, Celery Scheduling & Idempotency
author: kypkk

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: `wake_event.id` is used for Celery scheduling/Redis keying before the initial `flush()`. With SQLAlchemy `mapped_column(default=gen_uuid)`, the primary key typically isn’t populated until flush/insert, so this can schedule Job A with `None` (and also do extra scheduling work on duplicate inserts that later fail). Consider flushing first to obtain the id (and to surface uniqueness violations) and only then calling `apply_async`/saving the job id, still before `commit()`.

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: `alarm_id` is used directly in a UUID-typed comparison. If a client passes a non-UUID string, Postgres will typically raise an error during query execution (500) rather than returning a clean 404. Other services (e.g., alarm_service) validate UUIDs explicitly; consider adding a `UUID(alarm_id)` guard here to return a consistent 404/422 response.

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body:
`wake_event_id` isn’t validated before being used in a UUID-typed filter. If a client sends an invalid UUID, this can bubble up as a DB error (500). `get_wake_event()` already guards with `UUID(wake_event_id)`; recommend adding the same validation pattern in `respond_to_wake_event` (and similarly in `verify_wake_event`, `help_wake_event`, and `get_escalation_status`) to return a consistent 404.
```suggestion
    try:
        wake_uuid = UUID(wake_event_id)
    except ValueError:
        # Maintain consistency with get_wake_event: invalid UUID → 404
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=status.HTTP_404_NOT_FOUND,
            detail="Wake event not found",
        )

    result = await db.execute(
        select(WakeEvent)
        .where(WakeEvent.id == wake_uuid)
```

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: The PR description mentions the day-level idempotency guard (functional unique index on `(alarm_id, scheduled_time::date)`), but the test suite doesn’t currently assert behavior for “same alarm + same day + different timestamps”. Both _publish_to_family() and _save_job_c_id() create a new sync Redis client via from_url() for every call and then close it. _redis_client = sync_redis.from_url(settings.REDIS_URL)

```suggestion
    _redis_client.set(
        f"job:mark_failed:{wake_event_id}",
        task_id,
        ex=settings.ESCALATION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS + 60,  # buffer for clock skew
    )
```

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: The new Celery task wrappers (check_no_response/check_no_verify/mark_failed) include important behavior beyond the DB transitions: scheduling Job C via apply_async(), persisting the task id to Redis, and publishing Redis pub/sub events. review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: The websocket dependency is typed as RedisBroadcast, but get_broadcast_backend() is declared to return BroadcastBackend and websocket_service.handle_connection() also accepts BroadcastBackend. Keeping this parameter typed to the concrete RedisBroadcast makes the route harder to reuse (e.g., swapping to InMemoryBroadcast for dev/tests) and is inconsistent with the abstraction used elsewhere. review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body:
Dead socket cleanup removes broken WebSockets from the local registry, but it never unsubscribes from Redis (or deletes the channel key) when the last socket on a channel dies unexpectedly. This can leave the process permanently subscribed to channels with no active sockets, increasing Redis/pubsub load and memory usage over time. After removing dead sockets, if the channel’s connection list is empty, consider deleting it and calling pubsub.unsubscribe(channel) under the same lock.
```suggestion
            unsubscribed = False
            async with self._lock:
                for ws in dead:
                    try:
                        self._connections.get(channel, []).remove(ws)
                    except ValueError:
                        # Socket might already have been removed concurrently.
                        pass
                # After removing dead sockets, check if the channel still has any connections.
                remaining = self._connections.get(channel)
                if not remaining:
                    # Remove the empty channel entry and unsubscribe from Redis to avoid leaks.
                    self._connections.pop(channel, None)
                    try:
                        await self._pubsub.unsubscribe(channel)
                        unsubscribed = True
                    except Exception as e:
                        logger.exception(
                            "Failed to unsubscribe from Redis channel %s: %s",
                            channel,
                            e,
                        )
            if unsubscribed:
                logger.debug(
                    "Cleaned up %d dead socket(s) and unsubscribed from channel %s",
                    len(dead),
                    channel,
                )
            else:
                logger.debug(
                    "Cleaned up %d dead socket(s) on channel %s",
                    len(dead),
                    channel,
                )
```

title: feat: implement Celery escalation jobs with Redis broadcast
author: kypkk

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: `RedisBroadcast` is now the default backend used by the app, but the test suite only unit-tests `InMemoryBroadcast` and doesn’t cover the Redis pub/sub fan-out loop (`run_subscriber`). Adding at least a small integration/unit test (with Redis service already present in CI) would help catch regressions in subscription, message decoding, and dead-socket cleanup for the production path.

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: The Celery task retries on *any* exception, including failures in scheduling Job C / saving the task id / Redis publish. Since `_do_escalate` has already committed and changed the status, a retry will hit the guard clause and skip the side-effects, which can permanently drop the `escalation_started` broadcast (and potentially the Job C scheduling if the failure happened before `apply_async`). Consider making the post-transaction side-effects best-effort (log but don’t retry), or moving them into an idempotent/outbox-style mechanism so retries can safely re-attempt publishing/scheduling without being blocked by the guard clause.

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body:
Same retry/idempotency issue as above: `_do_mark_failed` commits the status change and user stat updates before the Redis publish. If the publish fails, `self.retry()` will run later but the guard will reject (status is already `failed`), so the `wake_resolved` broadcast may never be delivered. Handle Redis publish failures separately from the DB transition (e.g., best-effort publish or an outbox/retry mechanism that doesn’t depend on the status guard).
```suggestion
        # Retry the DB transition on failure.
        family_id = asyncio.run(_do_mark_failed(wake_event_id))
    except Exception as exc:
        logger.exception("mark_failed failed during state transition: wake_event=%s", wake_event_id)
        raise self.retry(exc=exc, countdown=10)

    if family_id:
        # Redis publish is best-effort and should not re-run the guarded DB transition.
        try:
            _publish_to_family(
                family_id,
                {
                    "event": "wake_resolved",
                    "wake_event_id": wake_event_id,
                    "status": "failed",
                },
            )
        except Exception:
            # Log and swallow publish errors to avoid losing the wake_resolved event
            # due to the status guard in _do_mark_failed on retry. Consider using
            # an outbox pattern for more robust delivery semantics.
            logger.exception(
                "mark_failed: failed to publish wake_resolved to family_id=%s wake_event=%s",
                family_id,
                wake_event_id,
            )
```

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body:
`_publish_to_family` / `_save_job_c_id` create a new Redis client on every call. In a long-running Celery worker this adds avoidable overhead (connection setup / pools) and can amplify failure rates under load. Prefer a module-level Redis client (or a small helper that reuses a single connection pool) and only close it on worker shutdown.
```suggestion
# Reuse a single Redis client across calls to avoid connection churn in workers.
_redis_client = sync_redis.from_url(settings.REDIS_URL)


def _publish_to_family(family_id: str, message: dict) -> None:
    """Publish a WebSocket event to all connected family members via Redis."""
    _redis_client.publish(f"family:{family_id}", json.dumps(message))


def _save_job_c_id(wake_event_id: str, task_id: str) -> None:
    """Persist Job C task ID so it can be revoked on success_with_help."""
    _redis_client.set(
        f"job:mark_failed:{wake_event_id}",
        task_id,
        ex=settings.ESCALATION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS + 60,  # buffer for clock skew
    )
```

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: The lifespan hook starts a background `run_subscriber()` task but never stores/cancels it on shutdown. With test fixtures using ASGITransport/TestClient (startup/shutdown per test), this can spawn many leaked subscriber tasks and/or multiple concurrent `listen()` loops against the same singleton backend. Store the created task (e.g., `app.state.redis_subscriber_task`) and cancel/await it on shutdown, and ensure the Redis connection/pubsub is closed.

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: `get_broadcast_backend()` is a module-level singleton and `lifespan()` starts `run_subscriber()` every time the app starts. In test runs (and any environment that instantiates the ASGI app multiple times), this can create multiple subscriber loops on the same `pubsub` object, which is not safe. Consider (a) making the backend instance app-scoped rather than module-global, and/or (b) adding an internal guard so `run_subscriber()` can only be started once per backend, plus a `close()` method to cleanly stop listening and disconnect.

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: The broadcast abstraction is effectively bypassed by changing `get_broadcast_backend()` to return `RedisBroadcast` and annotating the route dependency as `RedisBroadcast`. This makes it harder to swap backends (e.g., using `InMemoryBroadcast` in tests/local dev) and also exposes a method (`run_subscriber`) that isn’t part of the `BroadcastBackend` interface. Prefer keeping dependency types as `BroadcastBackend` and have `get_broadcast_backend()` return the interface (with a no-op `run_subscriber()` on the in-memory backend, or a separate startup hook specifically for Redis).

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: The dependency type was narrowed to `RedisBroadcast`, but `websocket_service.handle_connection` is written against the `BroadcastBackend` abstraction. Keeping the parameter annotated as `BroadcastBackend` (and importing that type) helps preserve the swappable-backend design and makes dependency overrides (e.g., `InMemoryBroadcast` in tests) more straightforward.

review_comments.body: The worker startup instructions don’t mention that the Celery app imports `settings = Settings()` which requires environment variables like `DATABASE_URL`, `JWT_SECRET`, and `REDIS_URL` to be set (or a `.env` present). Consider adding a short note here pointing back to “Setup” (copy `.env.example` -> `.env`) so `celery -A ... worker` doesn’t fail on missing settings.

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: `REDIS_URL` is still a required setting, but it’s not referenced anywhere in the Python codebase (no `settings.REDIS_URL` usages found). This means processes like the Celery worker will still fail to start unless `REDIS_URL` is provided, even though the worker now uses `CELERY_BROKER_URL`. Consider giving `REDIS_URL` a sensible default or making it optional until there’s code that actually consumes it.

author: GinoLin980

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: The auth_client fixture now tolerates a pre-existing user (409 -> login), which indicates the test DB can retain committed state across tests/runs. Since the API code commits transactions, the per-test session.rollback() will not reset committed rows, so this fallback can mask isolation issues and create order-dependent tests. Consider ensuring a clean DB per test run (e.g., drop/recreate or truncate tables) or wrapping each test in a SAVEPOINT/nested transaction instead of allowing 409 here.

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: These debug print(json.dumps(...)) statements add noise to the test suite output and can slow down runs when output capture is disabled. Please remove them (or gate them behind a failing assertion / use pytest's captured output on failure) so committed tests stay clean.

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: _register_and_auth decides whether to login by inspecting response JSON for a "token" key. This is brittle and can hide unexpected failures (e.g., a 422/500 would also lack "token" and trigger a login attempt). Prefer branching on explicit status codes (e.g., if register returns 409 then login) and assert expected status codes before reading token/user_id.

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body:
This helper falls back to login whenever the register response JSON lacks a "token" key, which can mask unexpected registration failures (422/500) and make tests harder to diagnose. Consider checking explicit status codes (e.g., 409 -> login) and asserting that register/login returned an expected status before reading resp.json()["token"].
```suggestion
    data = resp.json()

    # Successful registration should return a token.
    if resp.status_code in (200, 201) and "token" in data:
        token = data["token"]
    # If the user already exists, fall back to login.
    elif resp.status_code == 409:
        resp = await client.post("/auth/login", json={
            "email": email,
            "password": "password123",
        })
        assert resp.status_code == 200, f"Login failed: {resp.status_code} {resp.text}"
        login_data = resp.json()
        assert "token" in login_data, f"Login response missing token: {login_data}"
        token = login_data["token"]
    else:
        assert False, f"Unexpected register response: {resp.status_code} {resp.text}"
```

review_comments.author: Copilot
review_comments.body: register() does a pre-check for existing email, but doesn't handle the race where two requests register the same email concurrently. In that case the INSERT/COMMIT will raise an IntegrityError on the unique email constraint and currently bubble up as a 500. Consider catching sqlalchemy.exc.IntegrityError around commit/flush and translating it into the same 409 "Email already registered" response.

issue_comments.author: GinoLin980
issue_comments.body: also should we make a filter on `get_alarms` with `family_id` as it will now return all the alarms regardless the family

issue_comments.author: ShaoXiangChien
issue_comments.body:
Hey Gino, great work on this PR! 

A few things I really liked:
- The single JOIN query in get_family_detail with the correlated subquery for next_alarm_time is exactly the right approach. This will hold up well under morning traffic spikes.
- The UUID validation before DB queries in _assert_membership is a nice touch that prevents unhandled 500s.
- The invite code design comment explaining the alphabet choice and collision math is great engineering documentation. Keep doing this!
- The extra test_family_detail.py with edge cases for delay_minutes and next_alarm_time was beyond what was asked for. Really solid.

A couple of things to be aware of (I'll handle these in a follow-up branch so you don't need to change anything):  
- The rollback() + continue pattern in create_family can cause session state issues under production connection pooling
- In login, if an OAuth user tries to sign in with email/password, the error message just says "Invalid credentials"

Merging this in. Thanks for the solid work!
